title.ja: ホームラボでブログを運用する：理由と方法

description.ja: 自宅のサーバーで静的ブログを運用する理由、工夫、そして限界についての短いメモ。

children.text: ブログを運用する一番簡単な方法は、ホスティングサービスを使うことです。それでも私が自分のホームラボで動かしているのは、手を動かして学べるからです。Kubernetes、データベース、ネットワーク、セキュリティを一度に扱えます。
なぜ静的サイトなのか
読者が受け取るのはファイルだけなので、データベースが止まっていても記事は読めます。CMS が必要になるのは、記事を公開するときだけです。
停電や回線障害のときは、ミラーからサイトが配信されます
公開の瞬間を除いて、アプリケーションサーバーは動いていません
リリースはそれぞれ別々に保存されます
日本語の表示を確認します：長音記号（サーバー）、小書き文字（ちょっと、ファイル）、全角の句読点（、。）。

title.en: How this site is built: a static blog on a homelab

description.en: A headless CMS, a static Astro build, and nginx pods that keep serving even when the CMS is down. The reasoning and the trade-offs.

children.text: This site is a
static
Astro build. The words live in a headless CMS, but readers never touch it: they get plain files from
nginx
(or from a mirror in object storage when the homelab is down).
The shape of it
Publishing in the CMS triggers a build. The build produces a
dist/
folder, uploads it as a numbered release, and moves a pointer. The pods notice the new pointer and swap their content without a rollout.

fields.source:
direction: right
author: You { shape: person }
cms: Payload CMS
ci: GitHub Actions
r2: Object storage { shape: cylinder }
pods: nginx pods
author -> cms: publish
cms -> ci: dispatch
ci -> r2: upload release
pods -> r2: poll LATEST

children.text: How releases are laid out:
Static output, one folder per release
Pointer file names the live release
Rollback rewrites the pointer
Content-sync sidecar pulls the new release
Where the site build stands:
Type check clean
Pagination tried with a small page size
First real post written
Why not just render pages from the CMS?
Availability:
a static file keeps working when the database does not.
Cost:
no application runtime on the read path.
Security:
the CMS is only reachable behind an access gate.
A static site on a single-house homelab is strictly less available than a hosted static platform. The point of running it here is to learn, which is why a failover mirror exists.
Typed content, end to end
The schema is code. Types generated from it are imported by the site, so a schema change that breaks a page fails the type check before it fails a reader.
Building it
A local build is two commands:

title.en: What the homelab costs to run, in yen

description.en: A plain ledger of power, internet and storage costs for a small cluster, and the one number that decides whether it is worth it.

children.text: Running your own hardware is cheaper than renting it only if you count honestly. This is the ledger I keep, with
sample figures
in place of real ones.
The monthly ledger
Item
Basis
Monthly (¥)
Electricity
4 nodes, about 60 W total
Internet
Share of the home fibre line
Object storage
Free tier
Domain
¥1,800 a year
Total
Electricity is the line that moves. Japanese tariffs change with the season and the
, so I recalculate it every quarter.
Hardware, spread over its life
The mini PCs are paid for once. Divided over four years, they add a fixed amount to every month:
Hardware
Cost (¥)
Months
Per month (¥)
Mini PCs (×4)
Disks
The number that matters
About ¥5,470 a month, all in. The question is not whether that is cheap, but whether the learning is worth more than the equivalent managed services. For me it is.
